analysis.title: THINK Ahead: 3 ways the US midterms could reshape the global economy
key_insights: The US midterms on 3 November look likely to deliver divided government, with the House increasingly likely to fall to the Democrats and the Senate still on a knife edge. Gridlock makes domestic legislation harder and raises the importance of areas where the president can act alone, such as foreign policy and trade.

Middle East: a split or Democrat-run Congress could push Trump to focus on foreign policy, including the Iran war, while also inviting more congressional pushback, potentially over war-related funding. The new Congress does not take office until January, so the nearer question is what happens after Tuesday.

Markets are more worried about fresh US strikes on Iran after the midterms than about a diplomatic push to lower oil prices. JD Vance's letter to Iran this week was the clearest sign of diplomacy in some time, while reports of additional US military capabilities in the region point toward escalation.
If escalation does not materialise, ING's commodities team thinks some of the sizeable risk premium in energy prices could unwind.

Eurozone inflation could plausibly hit 4% next week and is biased higher while natural gas prices keep rising. ING expects elevated inflation until next summer, and the Bank of England is poised to hike next week for this reason.
AI: this week's strong US GDP data reflected AI-related investment rising by more than 20% year-on-year, while capex away from the AI build-out is still struggling for momentum.
AI is becoming a political issue. An Economist poll showed Democrat support surging this year among people living within 2km of a data centre, a group estimated at around 12 million Americans.

Federal consequences of the data centre backlash may be limited, since permitting is mostly a state and local matter and congressional attempts to unwind federal tax incentives could face a presidential veto. The midterms are a marker of how contentious the AI build-out could become before the 2028 presidential election, which matters given US equity markets' dependence on the AI story and shaky corners of the AI trade.

Fiscal: the US federal deficit is around 6% of GDP with little congressional appetite for consolidation. Last year's tax bill was a missed opportunity, and divided government makes a serious attempt over the next two years even less likely. The UK and Italy both released sensible budgets this week and look markedly better on public finances.

Trade: after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs, temporary 10% blanket rates gave way to a more permanent structure under Section 301. Tariffs have slipped down the agenda, but the president can raise them unilaterally, and Europe could be a target.

Tariffs matter for inflation and the Fed. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has repeatedly noted that roughly half of the inflation basket is running above 3%, and ING's analysis suggests tariffs explain a decent chunk of that. Refunds on the struck-down tariffs have started and have further to run, and over the summer they exceeded gross tariff revenue.

US week ahead: midterm elections on Tuesday and the October jobs report on Friday. All 435 House seats and 35 of 100 Senate seats are up. Polls show Democrats leading by around eight points nationally and Trump's approval at new lows.

ING expects October payrolls of around 75,000 with unemployment unchanged at 4.2%. Only a very soft outcome, potentially a negative print, would meaningfully move pricing for the 9 December Fed meeting, where markets price an 80% probability of a hike, which ING considers fair.

UK: ING expects a 7-2 Bank of England vote for a hike on Thursday, the first since the Iran War, and a follow-up hike in February. The hawkish risk is that the Bank explicitly signals further tightening.

Eurozone October inflation is released Wednesday. ING expects inflation to stay around 4% in coming months, with the focus on core and food prices for signs of second-round effects, which have so far been negligible. The ECB decides in December.

tension_points.bull_case: If diplomacy holds, as signalled by JD Vance's letter to Iran, some of the sizeable risk premium in energy prices could unwind, per ING's commodities team.
tension_points.bear_case: The US may prepare fresh strikes once the midterms pass and the political cost of higher gasoline prices eases. Reports of additional US military capabilities in the region point this way, and markets are more worried about this outcome.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Escalation not materialising after Tuesday's midterms would validate the energy risk premium unwind.
